summary: Extends the WebDAV MKCOL method so a client can create collections (folders) of types other than a plain one, and set properties on them in the same request. This makes it easier to create things like calendars or address books. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you can ask a server only for a plain folder. This lets you ask for a special kind of folder, like a photo album, and label it right away, all in one request.

what is the extended-mkcol dav header
subtitle: One WebDAV request that creates a folder of any special type and sets its properties at the same time.

tldr.problem: WebDAV extensions such as CalDAV needed 'special' collections and each invented its own MKxxx method, like MKCALENDAR, which adds server complexity and means every intermediary must learn the new method.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5689 lets the existing MKCOL method carry an XML body whose DAV:set elements give the properties for the new collection, including a DAV:resourcetype that picks its type.
tldr.outcome: Servers that support it advertise 'extended-mkcol' in the DAV header, and it can do the same job as MKCALENDAR. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4791 and RFC 4918.

today: RFC 5689 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4791 and RFC 4918.

sections.title: Why MKCOL Needed Extending
sections.content:
WebDAV (RFC 4918) defines the MKCOL method, which creates a collection on the server. Some WebDAV-based specifications, such as CalDAV (RFC 4791), define 'special' collections, identified by extra values in the DAV:resourcetype property or by other means.

Until now each of those got its own method, for example MKCALENDAR. The RFC says every new MKxxx method adds server complexity and hurts reliability, because intermediaries have to be made aware of it. The fix is to add a request body to MKCOL so the client can set properties as the collection is created, which avoids inventing new MKxxx methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new kind of folder used to need its own special request word. That is a lot of words to teach everyone, so this gives the one word 'make folder' the power to make any kind.

sections.title: The Extended MKCOL Request and Response
sections.content:
The request body is an XML document whose root is a single DAV:mkcol element. The Content-Type header MUST be set for an XML body, for example text/xml or application/xml. XML bodies with a different root element are reserved for future use.

Inside it, one or more DAV:set elements set properties on the collection as it is created. To create a collection of a particular type, DAV:resourcetype MUST be included in a DAV:set and MUST list the resource type elements, which MUST include DAV:collection.

The response is an XML document with a single DAV:mkcol-response element. It MUST contain DAV:propstat elements giving the status of each property when the request fails because one or more properties could not be set. On success the server MAY return a body that reports each property, and an empty body with a success status means all properties were set. In all other respects it behaves like standard MKCOL.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a little form saying what kind of folder you want and what to call it. The server sends back a note listing which items worked and which did not.

sections.title: All or Nothing, in Order
sections.content:
As with the PROPPATCH method, servers MUST process DAV:set instructions in document order. This is an exception to the normal rule that element order is irrelevant.

The instructions are atomic: either all succeed or all fail. If any error occurs, all executed instructions MUST be undone and a proper error returned. A failure to set a property value means the whole MKCOL fails, so the collection is not created.

The RFC adds a precondition, valid-resourcetype in the DAV: namespace, usually returned with 403 (Forbidden). It means the server MUST support the requested resource type for that collection.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like ordering a cake with a message on top: if the baker cannot write the message, you get no cake at all, not half a cake.

sections.title: Finding Out If a Server Supports It
sections.content:
A server that supports the feature MUST include extended-mkcol as a field in the DAV response header of an OPTIONS response, on any URI that supports extended MKCOL.

The RFC's example shows a response with DAV: 1, 2, 3, access-control, extended-mkcol. Clients can look for that token before sending a body-carrying MKCOL.
sections.plainLanguage: Before ordering, you can ask the server for its menu. If 'extended-mkcol' is on it, you can order the fancy folder.

sections.title: Examples: Success and Failure
sections.content:
In the success example, a client sends MKCOL for /home/special/ with a DAV:resourcetype containing DAV:collection and a made-up special-resource element, plus a DAV:displayname. The server answers 201 Created with no body.

In the failure example the server does not support that type. It answers 403 Forbidden with a DAV:mkcol-response. The resourcetype propstat carries the valid-resourcetype error, and the displayname propstat shows 424 Failed Dependency, because it was not applied either.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server knows your folder type, it says 'done'. If not, it says 'no' and also tells you the name label was not used since the whole order was cancelled.

sections.title: A Replacement for MKCALENDAR
sections.content:
The goal is to remove the need for other extensions to define their own MKCOL variants. If a server supports both this extension and the other one, it MUST support extended MKCOL to achieve the same result as the other extension's MKxxx method.

For CalDAV, MKCALENDAR creates a calendar collection and sets properties. The same effect comes from an extended MKCOL whose DAV:resourcetype contains both DAV:collection and CALDAV:calendar-collection. The RFC shows both requests side by side with equivalent properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a special 'make calendar' request, you use the normal 'make folder' request and say 'this folder is a calendar'. The result is the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says this extension does not introduce any new security concerns beyond those already described in HTTP (RFC 2616) and WebDAV (RFC 4918).
sections.plainLanguage: It does not add new ways to be unsafe beyond what the older rules already cover.
